title: Sweep Picking
goal: Sweep clean, separated arpeggios from two strings to five, in major, minor and diminished, and use them over a chord progression.
assumes: You can alternate-pick single notes evenly at sixteenths around 80 BPM (Alternate Picking through Step 6 covers this) and you can hammer on and pull off cleanly. You don't need any sweeping yet.

skills: Even alternate picking at sixteenths, 80 BPM

orderRationale: The owner's spine of two strings, then three, four and five, stays, because each added string is the honest unit of difficulty. Three things are woven into it. First, muting is taught from the first Exercise and never after, since it is what separates a sweep from a strummed chord, and bad habits here are hard to undo. Second, direction change gets its own Step between one-way three-string sweeps and more strings: turning around with a hammer and a pull is the hardest single idea, and it is cheapest to learn on three strings. Third, chord quality comes before more strings, with major first because its top-string reach is shorter, then minor, then diminished, so a player owns the shapes before stretching them. Six strings are left out on purpose: they add reach and little music at this level, and a later Path can add them. Moving between shapes is one Step and phrases are another, because a player who can only sweep one shape can't use it.
gradingLimits: Grading stops being trustworthy at about 150 ms between notes: sixteenths at 100 BPM, eighth triplets at 133, sextuplets at 66. Rungs faster than that are self-checked here, whatever they look like. That line is a cautious policy, not a measurement. No test anywhere covers swept notes, whose attacks are softer than picked ones and whose notes can ring on neighbouring strings. Even the graded rungs are provisional until there has been a real-guitar test. In practice: Steps 1 to 3 sit almost entirely under the line, the fast half of Steps 4 to 7 sits above it, and the fast sextuplet run in Step 8 and the top rungs of Step 9 are self-checked. Sound never tells us the two things that matter most here, muting and pick path, and the Exercises say so.

steps.title: Two strings, one stroke, and the mute
steps.goal: One continuous push of the pick through two strings, with two separate notes and nothing ringing.
steps.why: A sweep is one motion that plays several notes, which is why it is not alternate picking done faster. The smallest sweep is two strings, and it contains the whole technique: push through the first string, let the pick come to rest on the next, then push on. It also contains the whole problem: if the first note keeps ringing, you get a chord. Learn the mute now, while there are only two notes to keep apart.
howTo: Use a single push from the arm, with the wrist quiet. Think of a slow, heavy push rather than two small picks. The pick comes to rest on the next string between notes.
Fretting hand: as soon as the next note sounds, release the pressure on the last note without leaving the string. That is the left-hand mute, and it does most of the work.
Picking hand: keep the side of your palm on the lower strings, moving across with the sweep, so everything behind the pick stays silent.
Go slowly enough to hear two distinct notes. If you can't, it is too fast or a note is still ringing.
steps.payoff: A two-string lick you can play at any slow tempo and hear each note clearly, and a short pentatonic phrase that uses it.

exercises.title: Down through two strings
exercises.purpose: The motion on its own: down through the B and E strings, then stop.
howTo: Push through the B string and let the pick rest on the E string, then push through that. Stop for the rest and start again from above the B string.
exercises.coachLine: I can time the two notes and hear whether both were there. Listening for a ring between them is your job.

notes: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.

selfCheck: Record a take and listen back. Does each note stop as the next one starts, or do they ring together like a strummed chord?

exercises.title: Up through two strings
exercises.purpose: The same push going the other way. It is usually the weaker direction, and it won't get better unless you work on it alone.
howTo: From below the E string, push up through the E and B strings. Rest the pick against the next string up after each note.
exercises.coachLine: If this one comes out less even than the downward one, that is common. Give it a few more minutes.

exercises.title: There and back
exercises.purpose: Down through two strings, then up through the same two, with no gap. The top note repeats, so each direction is one whole stroke.
howTo: Two downs, then two ups, then rest. Note the stroke change on the repeated top note: that is the only moment the pick turns round.
exercises.coachLine: Evenness at these rungs tells us the pick is arriving on time. It can't tell which way it was moving.

exercises.title: Roll one finger across three strings
exercises.purpose: Fret 5 on three strings with one finger: the fingertip rolls so only the current note sounds. This is the fretting skill behind every barred sweep shape.
howTo: First finger across G, B and E at fret 5. Going up the strings, roll the fingertip so the finger leaves the last string as the next one sounds. Coming back, roll the other way.
Play it very slowly first with no click, and listen for two notes sounding together.
exercises.coachLine: Take this slowly. Notes bleeding into each other is what can't be measured yet, so a recording is your best check.

exercises.title: A two-string lick you can use
exercises.purpose: Two-string sweeps with a hammer and a pull, ending on D: the Step's audible payoff, and a phrase that already works in a solo.
howTo: Down through B and E, hammer to fret 8, pull back to 5, then up through the B string at fret 8, pull to 5, and finish on the G string.
Only the marked notes are picked. The hammer and pull give you notes for free.
exercises.coachLine: A quiet hammer or pull that I can't hear costs nothing, so don't dig in to please me.

steps.title: Three strings, each way
steps.goal: A clean one-way triad on the top three strings, at a tempo where each note can be told apart.
steps.why: Three strings is the first time a sweep sounds like one: three notes of a chord in one gesture. Keep it one-way for now so that all the attention is on the push and the mute, and so that you learn the shape as music rather than as a move.
howTo: Same single push, now through three strings. Keep the pick rest going: the pick lands on each string, then falls through it.
The Am shape at fret 14 uses first finger on the top string, second on the B string, third on the G string. Lift each finger's pressure as soon as the next note sounds.
Rest between sweeps. The rest is also a check: does anything keep ringing?
steps.payoff: You hear an actual arpeggio come out of one stroke, and you can play Am, F, C and G that way.

exercises.title: Am, downward only
exercises.purpose: The one gesture, repeated: one downward push across the Am shape, followed by a rest.
howTo: Triplets. Three notes, then silence for the same length. Bring the pick back above the G string during the rest, without touching anything.
exercises.coachLine: Three notes, spaced evenly, is what I'm able to check here.

exercises.title: Am, upward only
exercises.purpose: The upward push. Getting it to match the downward one is worth more than any speed you gain this week.
howTo: Start from below the top string. Pull up through E, B and G. Keep the same space between notes as you had going down.
exercises.coachLine: Compare this take with the downward one. They should sound like the same player.

exercises.title: Am, there and back
exercises.purpose: Up the strings and back, with the top note as the one turn: the shape of a real sweep, slowly.
howTo: Five notes and a rest. The stroke changes once, right after the top note. Keep that change as small as you can.
exercises.coachLine: When this one is even you're ready for a turnaround.

exercises.title: Am, F, C, G
exercises.purpose: Four triads in four shapes, one sweep each, so the shapes become chords you recognise rather than frets you remember.
howTo: Two sweeps per chord, one chord per bar. Move the hand during the rest and be there early.
exercises.coachLine: I can check the notes against each chord after the take, as long as they are separate enough to hear.

steps.title: Changing direction: the turnaround
steps.goal: Turn the sweep round at the top with a hammer and a pull, so it keeps flowing with no extra pick stroke.
steps.why: A sweep that goes one way is a trick. A sweep that goes up and comes back is a line, and the turn is where it usually falls apart: the pick is going down when the music needs it to come back. A hammer and a pull on the top string give the pick time to change direction without a stroke being heard. Learn it now on three strings, where there is little else to get wrong.
howTo: After the top string's push, the next note is a hammer-on, so the pick has nothing to do. Use that moment to turn it round.
The pull-off back is the last note before the upward push begins. Keep the pull clean: pull slightly sideways, off the string, and do not just lift.
Start with C major: its reach on the top string is three frets. The minor shapes reach five, and they come next.
steps.payoff: A triad that loops without a seam, with the turn inaudible, at a tempo you can sing along with.

exercises.title: C major, the short reach
exercises.purpose: The whole loop with the shortest top-string reach. G, C, E, then hammer to G and back.
howTo: Triplets. The first note of the loop after the first pass is an upstroke: the sweep comes back through it and turns, so you are never starting over.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say whether the notes were C major and how even they were. A quiet hammer does not count against you.

exercises.title: Am at fret 8
exercises.purpose: A minor shape with a four-fret reach. The same loop, and your little finger starts earning its keep.
howTo: First finger on fret 8 of the top string, second on fret 9 of the G, third on fret 10 of the B, little finger hammering at fret 12. One finger per note: no rolling on this shape.
exercises.coachLine: Same bar as the last one. If it slips, the stretch is the place to look.

exercises.title: Am at fret 12, the long reach
exercises.purpose: The classic shape, A, C, E and a five-fret hammer to A. Up here the frets are close enough that a five-fret reach is comfortable.
howTo: First finger on fret 12, little finger on 17. If the reach is too much for now, slide up to it instead: the sound is what counts.
exercises.coachLine: A clean turn on this shape is a real milestone. Check it on a recording too.

exercises.title: A turn with no hammer
exercises.purpose: Four notes with both ends turned by the pick alone, because you won't always have a hammer. It is the hard version: the pick really does change direction, twice.
howTo: Sixteenths. Stay small. After the bottom note, the next note is a downstroke, and after the top note, the next is an upstroke. Feel them as one elastic motion.
exercises.coachLine: This one gets fast quickly, and above the graded rungs it is yours to judge.

steps.title: Major, minor, then diminished
steps.goal: Play major, minor and diminished shapes on three strings, and hear exactly which note changes between them.
steps.why: A shape you can name is a shape you can use. Major and minor differ by one fret on one string, and that is the best ear training you can get on a guitar. Diminished comes last because it sounds tense and wants to go somewhere; it is what makes a sweep sound like the fast, dramatic thing you came to this Path for.
howTo: Name the notes out loud as you practise, at least once. The spelled notes on each Exercise are there for that.
Moving between inversions, shift during the last note of the bar, and arrive on the first finger of the new shape.
Diminished seventh shapes repeat every three frets with the same four notes. You only have to learn it once.
steps.payoff: You can hear a C major become C minor under your own fingers, and an A minor sweep resolving from its diminished neighbour sounds like the real thing.

exercises.title: C major becomes C minor
exercises.purpose: One fret, one string, a whole change of colour. E to Eb on the top string is the only move.
howTo: One bar of each. The note that changes is the third. Hear it before you play it.
exercises.coachLine: The notes against each chord are what I can check here. Listen for the colour yourself.

exercises.title: Am in three places
exercises.purpose: The same three notes in three shapes up the neck, so you can reach for Am wherever your hand happens to be.
howTo: Low shape is a one-finger barre roll at fret 5, the middle at fret 8 and the high at fret 12. Be ready on the new shape before the bar line.
exercises.coachLine: A shift is where notes go missing. If they do, look at the bar lines first.

exercises.title: C in three places
exercises.purpose: The major version, for the same reason. These three are what you'll move around when the chord changes.
howTo: Fret 8 shape, fret 12 shape, then the high shape from fret 15. Each one has a different lowest note: E, then G, then C.
exercises.coachLine: When this is as even as the minor one, the qualities are yours.

exercises.title: B diminished
exercises.purpose: A diminished triad, B, D, F, in the turn-with-the-pick form. It is the darkest sound on this Path, and it is only three notes.
howTo: No top note yet: both turns are pick turns. Hear how it wants to fall to C or A minor.
exercises.coachLine: I can check the three notes after the take. Whether it sounds dark and tense is for you to enjoy.

exercises.title: Diminished resolving to Am
exercises.purpose: Am to G# diminished 7 and back: the shape moves up three frets with the same notes, then resolves. This is the neoclassical sound in one line.
howTo: G#dim7 at fret 10 and Bdim7 at fret 13 are the same four notes, played from different places. Only the shape's position changes.
Hear the G# pull up to A at the end of the line.
exercises.coachLine: Well done if this sounds dramatic. That part is not something I measure, only that the notes are right.

steps.difficultyException: The tempo eases off slightly so the player can hear each quality and manage the shifts between shapes; those are the new demand here.

steps.title: Four strings
steps.goal: Add the D string without losing the separation you built on three.
steps.why: Four strings is enough for a full-sounding chord and short enough to keep clean. A longer push means more time for an earlier note to keep ringing, so it is the first real test of your muting. It's also the first place the pick travels far enough that the arm has to carry it, not the wrist.
howTo: Let the forearm carry the pick across. The wrist stays still.
The palm mute now has to travel with the pick, and the fretting hand keeps releasing each note in turn.
The bottom note is played once: you arrive on it with the upward push and leave it with a downstroke on the next string. Keep that change small.
steps.payoff: A sweep that sounds like a real chord being spelled out, at a tempo you can sing, in four shapes.

exercises.title: C major on four strings
exercises.purpose: The first four-string shape, with a short top reach and fingers that fall naturally.
howTo: Sixteenths, two loops a bar. From the second pass on, fret 10 on the D string is an upstroke that turns straight into a downstroke.
exercises.coachLine: Evenness and the right notes on the slow rungs. Above them, it is your own judgement.

exercises.title: Am on four strings
exercises.purpose: The Am shape with the D string underneath: the classic rock sweep, with the five-fret reach at the top.
howTo: Two fingers line up on fret 14, D and G strings, and you will have to roll between them. Keep that roll clean, as a stuck finger rings on.
exercises.coachLine: This shape tends to ring on the G and D strings. A recording shows it better than I can.

exercises.title: G major, the barre roll
exercises.purpose: Three strings on fret 12 under one finger. It's a rolling problem more than a picking one, so it's your check on the fretting-hand mute.
howTo: Roll across fret 12, then drop to fret 10 on the top string with your first finger. You will need to re-think which finger goes where, and that's fine: the sound is what matters.
exercises.coachLine: I can check the notes if they are separate enough. If I can't, that is useful to know too.

exercises.title: Am, F, C, G on four strings
exercises.purpose: One bar each, and the shapes must arrive on time. This is the test of whether four-string shapes are yours.
howTo: Sixteenths. The hand moves in the last note of each bar. All the shapes are within a few frets of each other, so the moves are short.
exercises.coachLine: When this one is even you are in good shape for five strings.

steps.title: Five strings: the root positions
steps.goal: Own the two common five-string shapes with the root on the A string, in minor and major.
steps.why: Five strings is the big sweep, the sound people mean when they say the word. There are few shapes to learn: minor from the A string, major from the A string, and the two moved around. Everything else on the fretboard is one of those at a different fret, which is why you learn only these.
howTo: Minor: root on the A string, a hammer to the third on that same string, then one note a string up to the top. Major: a chord tone below the root, hammer to the root, then one note a string.
Mute everything. With five strings moving there is more to keep silent than there are fingers: palm on the low strings, fretting fingers across the high ones.
Keep this below your speed limit. A clean five-string sweep at a modest tempo sounds better than a fast smear.
steps.payoff: The sound you came for: a five-string arpeggio up the neck and back, with every note separate.

exercises.title: A minor, the classic
exercises.purpose: A, C, E, A, C, E, A on five strings, with the turn at each end. The most-used shape on this Path.
howTo: Triplets, one loop a bar. Hammer at the bottom, hammer and pull at the top. The last note on the A string is an upstroke that pulls off into the first note of the next loop.
exercises.coachLine: Up to the graded rungs I can check notes and evenness. Above that the tempo is yours to judge, on a recording.

exercises.purpose: Major: G hammered up to C, then E, G, C, E and a three-fret top reach. It is a wider shape at the bottom and easier at the top.
howTo: The reach from fret 10 to 15 on the A string is your widest. Warm up before pushing on this one.
exercises.coachLine: The same bar as Am. Compare the takes.

howTo: Ten triplets, then a rest for two. There is no bottom hammer here, so you turn with the pick. Use the rest to reset.
exercises.coachLine: A rest at the end of each loop makes these notes easier to tell apart too.

exercises.title: E minor, lower down the neck
exercises.purpose: The Am shape down at fret 7, where the top reach becomes a slide. Lower frets are wider, and you should know what to do when the hammer no longer reaches.
howTo: Slide up from fret 7 to 12 on the top string, and slide back. A slide is a good choice wherever the frets are too wide for a clean hammer.
exercises.coachLine: A slid-to note can be too quiet for me to catch, and the bar on this one allows for that. Judge the slide by ear.

steps.title: Moving shapes
steps.goal: Change five-string shape at the bar line with no gap and no lost notes.
steps.why: You now have shapes, and music asks for them in a hurry. A real progression doesn't wait while you find the next one, so this Step is where the shapes you own become usable: the hand travels in the time of one note, and the sweep picks up as if nothing happened.
howTo: Look at the next shape before you need it. The eye gets there first, then the hand.
Most of these moves happen in the last note of the bar. Let that note go, and be early rather than late.
Practise only the move first: the last two notes of the bar and the first two of the next.
steps.payoff: A real four-chord progression played entirely in big sweeps.

exercises.title: Am down to Dm
exercises.purpose: A big move of seven frets between two minor shapes. It is an obvious, musical change, and a good test of how far the hand can travel.
howTo: Am at fret 12, Dm at fret 5. Note the Dm's slide at the top: frets down there are too wide to hammer.
exercises.coachLine: A large shift is where the first note after it goes missing. Check that note after the take.

notes: Swept notes have soft attacks and can ring into each other. Detection of them is unproven, so only slow rungs are graded and the fast ones are self-checked.
Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.

selfCheck: Record a take and listen back. Does each note stop as the next one starts, or do they ring together like a strummed chord?

exercises.title: Am, F, C, G
exercises.purpose: The same progression as the last Step, on five strings, so you hear how much bigger the same chords sound.
howTo: F and G have ten notes and a rest of two. Use the rest to move. Am and C have twelve notes, so those moves come in the last note of the bar.
exercises.coachLine: Slower and clean beats fast and rough. This one is worth repeating at a rung that stays even.

exercises.title: Dm, G, C, Am on four strings
exercises.purpose: Dm, G, C is the circle of fifths, played in shorter shapes. It uses less travel, and it comes round like a tune, so your ear can follow if your hands get lost.
howTo: Sixteenths, two loops a chord. Sing the top note of each shape if you can. They make a melody.
exercises.coachLine: At these speeds the app grades only the slow rungs. Your ear has to decide about the fast ones.

steps.title: Sweeps inside phrases
steps.goal: Use a sweep as part of a line that goes somewhere, starting and ending in a scale or on a held note.
steps.why: Nobody wants to hear ten bars of arpeggio. What makes a sweep sound exciting is what comes either side of it: a line that arrives by sweep, then sings; a run that shoots up to a held bend. This Step turns the shapes into something you could actually play in a solo.
howTo: The held note after a sweep matters more than the sweep. Give it time and a little vibrato.
Change technique cleanly. When a sweep ends, you go straight back to normal picking, with no moment of confusion in the hand.
Use these as starting points. Write your own ending as soon as you can play the written one.
steps.payoff: Four phrases you can actually use in a solo, each one ending in a note that sings.

exercises.title: Sweep up, scale down
exercises.purpose: Up the Am shape, then run back down the scale with pull-offs. It is the most natural sweep phrase there is, and it ends on a held A with vibrato.
howTo: Hammer to 17, then three pull-offs on the top string (each pull sounds the next note), then pick the run down the B and G strings.
exercises.coachLine: A chain of pull-offs may be too quiet for me, and that's fine. It's the picked notes I can check.

exercises.title: Two strings, a run, and a bend
exercises.purpose: Your two-string lick from Step 1, extended with a three-string start and finishing in a whole-tone bend. It ties the whole Path back to where it began.
howTo: Sweep through G, B and E, then the lick. The last note is D on the G string, bent up to E and held with vibrato. Hear E on the B string first, so you know where the bend has to reach.
exercises.coachLine: I can check the picked notes. How far the bend went is up to your ear: compare it with the E at fret 5 on the B string.

A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: Record a take and listen back. Does each note stop as the next one starts, or do they ring together like a strummed chord?
Did the bend reach the same pitch as the E on the B string, fret 5?

exercises.title: Am up, G down
exercises.purpose: Two triads in one gesture: Am up the strings, G back down. Together they give a modern, open sound, and you only have to know one small shape each.
howTo: Three up, pull off to fret 10, two more upstrokes down the strings. Loop it. It works over A minor or over a G chord, and hearing that is worth a minute.
exercises.coachLine: Short and repeatable: this is a good one for the top of the ladder, which you'll judge by ear.

exercises.title: A fast sweep as a pickup
exercises.purpose: A long, held note, then one beat of fast sweep into the next bar. It is the sound of a sweep used sparingly, and it's where this Path's grading stops being trustworthy, even at these low tempos.
howTo: Sextuplets in the fourth beat only. Aim for the next downbeat. If the sextuplet is not perfect, the landing will still save the phrase.
exercises.coachLine: Sextuplets are fast enough that I can only grade the slowest rungs, and even those are unproven. Trust your own ear above them.

steps.difficultyException: Held notes pull the average rate well down. The new demand is changing technique mid-phrase and making it musical, which the metric does not count.

steps.title: Over a chord progression
steps.goal: Play sweeps that follow Am, F, C, G over a band, from three strings up to five, and one chorus you put together yourself.
steps.why: Everything so far has been against a click. A band is different: the bass already plays the root, so your arpeggio can start somewhere else, and the drums will happily cover you if you get lost for a beat. This is where it stops being an exercise and sounds like what you hoped to play.
howTo: Keep the volume honest: if the band is covering your mistakes, turn it down until they show.
Use direct input or headphones for a graded take. A microphone also hears the band, and that hasn't been tested.
Start each version at a rung where you can look up from the guitar. You're playing with people now, even if the people are samples.
steps.payoff: You play a sweep arpeggio solo over a band, and it follows the chords.

exercises.title: With the band: three strings
exercises.purpose: The three-string shapes, one per chord. Short enough to stay clean, and the first time you hear your own sweep sitting on a progression.
howTo: Two loops a bar. Lock the first note of each bar to the kick and let the rest fall into place.
exercises.coachLine: Band in the room, so direct input if you want these numbers to mean something.

exercises.title: With the band: four strings
exercises.purpose: The same progression at sixteenths on four strings. Here the graded rungs end while the tempo is still comfortable, so the top of the ladder is on your ear.
howTo: Two loops a bar, at a tempo the band can really sit in. Up to about 100 BPM the app can help. Above that, record and listen.
exercises.coachLine: I can help on the slow rungs. Above them, a recording will tell you more than I can.

exercises.title: With the band: five strings
exercises.purpose: The big shapes through the whole progression. Keep it at a tempo where every note is separate: at this length, a smear is obvious.
howTo: One loop a bar, with Am and C at twelve notes, and F and G at ten and a rest. Use the rests to move.
exercises.coachLine: On the rungs I grade, this is the hardest thing on the Path. Above them it is yours alone, and it is meant to be.

exercises.title: Your own eight bars
exercises.purpose: A written example chorus that mixes three-string shapes, five-string shapes and a phrase ending. Learn it, then replace any bar with your own. Nothing here is graded, on purpose.
howTo: Record it. Listen for the moments where it sounds like music and the moments it sounds like an exercise. Change the second kind.
exercises.coachLine: No score on this one. It's your chorus, so you decide when it's done.
